entries.text: Headline result: supervised classifiers averaged 16-21% overall accuracy on 38-way intended-phoneme discrimination, vs 1/38 (2.6%) chance.

questions.q: What are the headline classification numbers and how do they compare to chance?
questions.answer: LDA 16.9%, SVM 21.0%, FDA 17.6% overall accuracy (Table 3), all above the 1/38 (0.0263, ~2.6%) one-tailed binomial chance level (p<0.05). Per-phoneme success was non-uniform: 20 of 38 phonemes above chance for all three classifiers, 26 for at least one.

questions.q: On what data were these numbers computed, and what was excluded?
questions.answer: 431 trials over five sessions (subset of 59 sessions over 10 months, excluding sessions with technical problems or biofeedback), 10-12 repetitions per phoneme, phoneme 24 (/f/) dropped for insufficient trials. Single male LIS subject (ventral-pons brainstem stroke 9 years prior, automobile accident), implanted 2004-12-22, age 25 at study.

questions.q: Is the evaluation held out, or within-sample cross-validation? Are seeds and per-class chance levels reported?
questions.answer: Within-sample only: 10-fold CV on the same 431 trials (randomly partitioned; trial-level split, grouping/leakage across same-session siblings unspecified). No independent test set, seeds, bootstrap counts, or exact per-phoneme chance probabilities are reported.

questions.q: Can the participant's attempted phonemes be verified at all, and is response timing known?
questions.answer: No. LIS precludes instantaneous observable behavior; timing and identity of attempts rest on cued stimuli plus post-trial self-report accepted/rejected by the experimenter. The classifier is applied to fixed 10-s windows that likely contain non-attempting segments.

questions.q: Are the reported accuracies good enough for a functional speech BMI?
questions.answer: Not for a communication device, per the authors themselves ('truly not great enough to be useful as a communication device'). The study is off-line only; no closed-loop or online latency/throughput was measured, and the 300 ms analysis delay may be too slow for conversational speech.

questions.q: Which phonemes were classified above chance, and is the pattern non-uniform?
questions.answer: Yes, strongly: LDA 24/38 (3/9 vowels, 3/6 diphthongs, 18/23 consonants), SVM 24/38 (5/9, 3/6, 16/23), FDA 22/38 (4/9, 2/6, 16/23); 20 above chance for all three, 26 for any. Consonants (especially lip-involving and voiced) classified best; rounded/front vowels best among vowels.

questions.q: Are there stimulus or label confounds?
questions.answer: Yes: stop consonants are presented as CVs with minimized trailing vowel (not all CV combinations used); stimuli are 200 ms excerpts of the participant's father's exemplars, not the participant's own voice (44.1 kHz wav); the execute-vs-imagine hypothesis was not tested.

questions.q: What do the authors concede as limitations?
questions.answer: Accuracy insufficient for a communication device; findings may be subject-specific and not generalize; timing/identity of attempts unverifiable; noise from spike clustering and user-response uncertainty; diphthongs excluded from articulatory ANOVA; functional-BMI usefulness unevaluated; static classifiers may need dynamic models (HMMs).

questions.q: Is there any evidence the decoded signal reflects speech articulation rather than generic motor activity?
questions.answer: Only indirect/correlational: significant ANOVA main effects for tongue height/location/rounding (vowels) and voicing/manner/articulator (consonants), p<0.001; front vowels, rounded vowels/lip consonants, voiced consonants classified best. No causal or overt-behavior evidence exists (LIS); the execution-vs-imagery hypothesis was untested.

questions.q: Was any code or data released with the paper?
questions.answer: No public code or data is linked anywhere in the paper (R packages MASS, mda, e1071 and Matlab were used; no repository or dataset is referenced). There is nothing to fetch; reproducibility depends entirely on the 431 raw trials held by the authors.

questions.q: Were single-unit and multi-unit signals distinguished, and are sorting quality metrics reported?
questions.answer: No distinction was made or reported: 31 manually sorted convex-hull clusters (peak/valley amplitude, height, energy, alignment-point amplitude) were pooled; no cluster-separation/false-alarm metrics, no ablation, and no per-cluster contribution analysis are given.

questions.q: How was statistical significance assessed, and is multiplicity handled?
questions.answer: One-tailed exact binomial tests against per-phoneme chance with bootstrapped empirical distributions, Bonferroni-corrected to p<0.05 for the 38 per-class tests. No confidence intervals on overall accuracies; obvious caveat: binomial tests assume independent trials, while trials within a session are not demonstrably independent.

questions.q: Does the paper compare against the only other invasive speech-decoding human work (ECoG)?
questions.answer: Yes, as framing, not as a head-to-head benchmark: prior ECoG studies decoded 4 phonemes (Blakely 2008) and 10 words (Kellis 2010); this study scales intracortically to 38 phonemes and contrasts 300 ms bins vs Kellis's 500 ms prediction delay, but it does not re-analyze those datasets or transfer models across subjects.

questions.q: Is the classification sample a 300-ms bin or a trial, and are bins of one trial kept in one fold? Are clusters stable across sessions? What verifies the attempt? Any rest or shuffled control?
questions.answer: Bins are the samples (180-216 per phoneme), randomly partitioned into 10 folds with no trial grouping stated; sorting parameters from one off-line analysis were reused across sessions; the attempt rests on instruction plus post-trial denial; no rest or shuffled-label control.
